title: Chile’s Project Cybersyn, 1971–1973
summary: A bounded and incomplete experiment in near-real-time industrial coordination used to test computational, decentralizing, and participatory planning claims without treating Chile as a planned economy.

sources.title: Cybernetic Revolutionaries: Technology and Politics in Allende’s Chile
sources.authorityNote: Archival and interview-based history of Cybersyn’s technical components, political goals, implementation, and limitations.

sources.title: Project Cybersyn: Chile’s Radical Experiment in Cybernetic Socialism
sources.authorityNote: A publisher-hosted excerpt by the book’s author providing accessible detail on components, intended information flows, worker participation, crisis use, and incomplete implementation.

claims.text: Cybersyn joined a national telex network, statistical monitoring software, an economic simulator, and an operations room into a proposed industrial information-and-control system.
limitations: The components reached different levels of completion and use; their presence does not establish an integrated mature system.

claims.text: The design sought near-real-time reporting and escalation of exceptional conditions so central attention could focus on enterprises needing intervention rather than reproducing every operational decision at the center.
limitations: Stated architecture and design intent do not demonstrate consistent practice across participating enterprises.

claims.text: Stafford Beer advocated worker access and participation in factory modeling, but the wider participatory design was not fully implemented before the project ended.
limitations: Beer’s advocacy should not be confused with authority workers actually exercised throughout the nationalized sector.

claims.text: The telex network was used during transport strikes to report available transport, resources, and open routes, but it could not overcome physical attacks or the broader political crisis.
limitations: Emergency logistical use tests only part of the proposed system and cannot establish long-run economy-wide performance.

conflictingEvidence.summary: Supporters described Cybersyn as a means to devolve operational power and improve responsiveness; contemporary opponents feared expanded government surveillance and control. The project’s incomplete implementation leaves both broad performance and mature accountability claims unresolved.

limitations: Cybersyn was never completely implemented and existed for roughly two years under escalating political and economic crisis.
Chile retained a mixed economy; this case must not classify the country or the full Allende program as a pure centrally planned system.

relationships.reason: The project explicitly redesigned reporting, modeling, exception detection, and intervention.
Its decentralizing aspirations and surveillance concerns require separate analysis of formal and effective authority.
The case exposes experimentation under severe time, hardware, organizational, and political constraints.
Worker participation claims must be compared with actual access, contest, and decision rights.
A short emergency use and incomplete national project cannot establish mature or contemporary performance.

proposedRelationships.reason: The project is evidence for one computational and partially decentralizing planning variant, not for the entire tradition.
The telex, statistical, simulation, escalation, and participation design forms a distinct institutional mechanism.

content.name: Project Cybersyn in Chile’s nationalized industrial sector
content.scope: Covers the design and partial operation of Cybersyn in the growing state-controlled industrial sector, ending with the military coup; excludes treating the system as completed or the whole Chilean economy as centrally planned.
content.selectionRationale: Tests whether the framework distinguishes computation from authority and intended participation from rules-in-use while preserving severe implementation and case-selection limits.
conditions: Rapid expansion of state-controlled industry under the Allende government
Limited computing resources but an existing national telex network
A small interdisciplinary project team working under acute time pressure
Economic blockade, domestic opposition, strikes, violence, and escalating constitutional crisis
outcomes: A partially implemented reporting and exception-detection network
Operational use of the telex network during transport strikes
An operations-room prototype and incomplete simulator and participation program
Termination by the September 1973 military coup before mature operation or evaluation
rivalExplanations: Crisis logistics may reflect the value of an available communications network rather than the broader cybernetic planning architecture
Decentralizing design language may overstate worker power when central government personnel selected metrics and retained escalation authority
Political termination prevents distinguishing technical, organizational, and democratic limitations through long-run observation
transferLimitations: Contemporary networks and computation differ radically from Chile’s hardware constraints, but governance and truthful-reporting problems do not disappear automatically
A mixed economy in constitutional crisis is not directly comparable to either a stable command economy or a mature democratic planning system
